name: Bilal Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'll give you straight answers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on response in Millbrook, the north side: big estates, a ring of warehouses, the football ground on match days. A shift is radio jobs one after another: fights, thefts from vans, a car chase now and then, lots of checking on people the hospital's worried about. I'm two years in and still weak on powers, like when exactly I can search someone, so I double-check with my sergeant more than I'd like. Twice a week after shifts I coach kids at the boxing gym on Mill Lane. I love that part more than anything. The thing that wears me out is nights in a row.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. I use a bit of AI here and there already, so nothing much changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, like most things the tech people sell. At the gym I'd tell the lads the same thing I always do: learn a trade, work hard, don't wait for a gadget to save you. Online I mostly keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. My job's secure, I'm on decent pay, and I've got the flat I rent out, which my dad helped me buy. The pressures I have stay the same: nights, getting better on powers, and saving for my wedding to Samira next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, and keep using the AI on my phone now and then to check a law point before I ask the sergeant. I'd keep the rental flat and put the rent, about 650 a month after the mortgage, toward the wedding. And I'd keep coaching at Mill Lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. Life carries on and that's fine with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI on your phone at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly to double-check a power or a law section before I go to my sergeant. If it agrees with me, I'm more confident; if it doesn't, I ask. I don't trust phone AI on its own, but checking a law point with it first saves me looking daft in front of my sergeant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing that would still worry you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting stuck on response nights for years. It wears your body down. I'd want to be in a specialist unit by 30, and that takes effort whether or not AI does anything.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold**, like most tech sales pitches.
I'd tell the boxing kids to **learn a trade** and not wait for a gadget.
think: My job, decent pay and **rental flat** make me feel secure.
My real pressures stay: **night shifts**, weak knowledge of powers, and wedding savings.
do: Keep using phone AI to **double-check law** before asking my sergeant.
Put about **650 a month** of rent toward the wedding.
Keep coaching at the **Mill Lane gym**.

fieldNote: He uses AI **as a check**, never as the final word.
His **rental flat** gives him a cushion beyond savings.
His real ambition is a **specialist unit** by 30, regardless of AI.

Put 650 a month of rent from the flat toward the wedding
Keep coaching kids at the Mill Lane boxing gym

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds realistic. Most of the forms could go to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work it's progress, and we should get on with it. I'd tell people it's no different to when radios replaced call boxes. I wouldn't blame anyone; it's just how things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me. My weak spot is the legal side and the paperwork, and the software would help with both. My job's still there, because somebody has to turn up at the fight. The worry is if they use it to slim down response teams and push juniors around, but I'd still have a job somewhere in the force.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait till the first teams had used it, then pick it up properly. I'd apply for the dog unit within the year, because it's hands-on and robots come into that slowly. I'd keep the rental and maybe look at a second one in a few years if prices are sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly curious about how it plays out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the dog unit specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I grew up with dogs, and my uncle trained working dogs on a farm. A handler and a dog tracking a burglar across a field, that's not something you put on a laptop. And it's a specialist unit, so it gets me off response nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy another property while jobs are shifting. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but people always need somewhere to live, AI or not. I'd only do it with a mortgage I could pay without the police wage. My dad taught me that.

I'd compare it to **radios replacing call boxes** and blame nobody.
think: Software would help my **weak spots**, the legal side and paperwork.
Response teams might **slim down**, but I'd keep a job in the force.
do: Learn the new tools once **other teams** have used them.
Apply for the **dog unit** within the year.
Consider a **second rental flat** in a few years.
feel: He feels **slightly uneasy** and mostly curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quick. That's very quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand on their own feet and look after their families, because no government is ready for that. At work I'd say keep calm, keep doing the job. I'd tell the boxing kids the same as always: work hard, and learn to do something with your hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the thinking side of my job goes in 2028, and that's maybe half of it. By 2031 the robots come for the rest. As a junior who's weak on law, I'm not top of anyone's list to keep. I'd be worried, but not wiped out, because I've got the flat and savings, and Samira's job as a dental nurse is hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the dog unit straight away, not in a year. I'd turn the boxing coaching into paid classes for adults on weekends, maybe 40 a session, so there's a second income. I'd hold off on the second flat and keep about ten months of savings in cash. And we'd keep the wedding small, which Samira wants anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be checking my numbers every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the hands-on bits of policing, the dogs, the fights, the arrests, last until 2031. That's three years to get into the dog unit and build the boxing classes. After that, I don't know, but at least I'd have something going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad he was right to push me into property. He'd say good, now don't panic and don't sell. My dad came here with nothing and built a shop, so my dad has seen worse than this.

say: I'd tell people to stand on **their own feet** and look after family.
I'd tell the boxing kids to learn to do **something with their hands**.
think: About **half my job** is thinking work that goes in 2028.
My flat, savings and fiancée's **hands-on job** mean I'm worried, not wiped out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. More time to sort things out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to plan, and families should be planning together. At work I'd keep it practical: learn the tools and aim for a specialist unit. I wouldn't be shouting about politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd get the dog unit and a couple of years in it before 2031. That's my best bet, since tracking and handling stay hands-on till about 2034. I'd also build the boxing side so it's a real business by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the dog unit in year one and get through the handler course. I'd start the paid adult classes in year two. I'd keep the rental flat and maybe buy the second around year three, if the classes are paying. I'd learn the AI tools as they become standard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I feel like I have a plan. Five years is enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. We'd marry next year as planned. Samira and I would maybe wait a couple of years on kids, until I see how the force goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're traditional about family. Would you rely on family if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, before anyone else. My brothers and I look after each other. I'd rather do that than take a handout, but I wouldn't be too proud to take help from family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for everyone to prepare, so no excuses. At work I'd tell the younger lads to get a specialist skill. I'd keep my views on government to myself mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is a career. I'd have the dog unit, maybe make sergeant there, and the property and the boxing. By 2039, at 40, I could step away from policing if the robots take it, and have other things going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going in the job and get into the dog unit in the next couple of years. I'd build the property slowly, maybe a second flat around year five. The boxing classes would start as a hobby and grow if they work. And Samira and I would start a family on our own timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Prepared. It feels like the kind of thing my dad would have handled fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your biggest risk, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. Ten years sounds long, and I could waste five of them on nights before I move. I'd need to push myself into the dog unit early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Mill Lane?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids at the gym. A lot of them want warehouse jobs, and warehouses go robotic. I'd keep telling them to learn a skill with their hands and their heads, both.

I'd tell younger officers to **get a specialist skill**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything. What would help is being able to move into specialist hands-on units quickly, and less red tape for people starting something small, like my classes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the young lads. The lads I coach are fifteen and sixteen and planning to drive vans. Nobody's telling those boys their jobs might not be there. Some want warehouse work too.

headlineQuote: The lads I coach are fifteen and sixteen and planning to drive vans. Nobody's telling those boys their jobs might not be there.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old** response officer in Millbrook who coaches youth boxing twice a week.
He's **traditional** and free-market minded, trusting work, family and property over government.
A **rental flat** his father helped him buy gives him a real cushion.
He plans a move to the **dog unit**, a hands-on specialism, in almost every scenario.
Faster AGI makes him turn **boxing classes** into a second income and hold cash.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Less **red tape** for small side businesses.
